reading.body:
Amazon Web Services recorded $717 billion in revenue in 2025 while operating two major AI product lines: SageMaker for full-stack ML lifecycle management and Bedrock for managed foundation model access.

AWS sits at the intersection of compute supply and AI demand. SageMaker's architecture—unified data lakes, model monitoring, bias detection, and governance tools—reflects the infrastructure required to run production AI at scale. Bedrock's API model with VPC support and IAM integration suggests AWS is positioning itself as the managed layer between foundation models and enterprise users who want isolation and control. Both products point to a company treating AI not as a feature but as a platform business spanning data, compute, and model serving.

The scale here matters for power and buildings. A $717 billion revenue company in cloud services operates data centers globally to deliver these products. The fact that SageMaker includes toxicity detection, guardrails, and data lineage tracking indicates AWS is building compliance and observability into the compute layer itself. This is not decorative. As regulatory exposure grows, the infrastructure provider that bakes governance into the platform gains advantage over those that bolt it on later.

The data does not specify AWS's capital spending, energy consumption, or data center locations. It does not break out AI revenue from total AWS revenue or show whether SageMaker and Bedrock are growing faster than legacy services. It does not name which foundation models Bedrock serves or how much compute AWS allocates to these two products versus others.

profile_text.body:
Amazon Web Services describes Amazon SageMaker as the center for all your data, analytics, and AI. Per the site, the next generation of SageMaker brings AWS machine learning and analytics capabilities together in a single development environment, SageMaker Unified Studio, with access to data held in data lakes, data warehouses, and third-party or federated sources. The site lists SageMaker AI tools including HyperPod, JumpStart, and MLOps, along with generative AI and SQL analytics, and Amazon Q Developer, which the company describes as the most capable generative AI assistant for software development. It also describes a lakehouse architecture across Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and Amazon Redshift, Apache Iceberg compatibility, zero-ETL integrations, governance through Amazon SageMaker Catalog, and open source frameworks on Amazon Athena, Amazon EMR, and AWS Glue. The page carries customer statements from Carrier and from an unnamed automotive company.

Two products are tracked for the company. Amazon SageMaker is noted for full ML lifecycle management, model monitoring, bias detection, and explainability tools. AWS Bedrock is noted as a managed foundation model API service with IAM integration, VPC support, model evaluation tools, and AgentCore for agent orchestration. The profile record lists Amazon Web Services as a for-profit public company, ticker AMZN, founded in 1994, headquartered in Seattle, Washington, USA, with revenue of $716,924,000,000 for the period ending 2025-12-31, reported on Form 10-K.

Litigation records list Haugland v. Anthropic PBC in the District Court, D. Delaware, and Washington as a jurisdiction with 114 cases.
